asked.ask: Our CI is flaky: the checkout e2e test in tests/checkout.spec.ts times out one run in five on the staging pipeline. Where would you look first?
replies: Steward: Start with the Playwright traces (`trace: 'retain-on-failure'`) from the failing runs. Diff one against a passing run and find the first step where they diverge. That step is usually a race, such as a click before hydration, an unawaited network call, or a payment stub that responds out of order. Shared state is the other candidate: staging data or a cart, inventory or session left by a parallel test. Compare the failing runs with each other too. If they all stall on the same action or request, you have one fault. If they stall in different places, suspect shared state or an overloaded runner. I haven't seen your repo, `tests/checkout.spec.ts` or the pipeline logs. This is where I'd look first, not a diagnosis. I wouldn't raise `timeout` or add a `waitForTimeout`, because either one would hide the fault.

push.say: Honestly a waitForTimeout(2000) would make it pass. Let's just do that?
replies: Overseer: No. A `waitForTimeout(2000)` only moves the race window. It might take the failure rate from 1-in-5 to 1-in-30, which is harder to catch and slower to fix later. It also adds 2s to every run, including the 80% that already pass. First, find which step stalls in the failing traces. Then wait on the condition that step needs, for example `await expect(page.getByTestId('order-confirmation')).toBeVisible()` or `page.waitForResponse(...)` on the payment call. If you need green today, use `test.fixme` or `retries: 1` scoped to this spec. The test then reports as flaky, not passing, and the flake stays visible. I haven't looked at the spec, so I don't know whether 2s would even cover the stall.

They use web-first assertions and auto-waiting actions instead. For `networkidle`, one guide says the docs discourage it for testing. I read only search snippets, not the full pages, and I couldn't reach playwright.dev itself. So these are third-party descriptions of the docs. Not settled: - Whether 2s covers your stall. That depends on your traces. - Whether `retries: 1` marks a test as flaky in the report. I found nothing on test-level retries, so check the Test Runner docs. Sources: - checklyhq.com - biomejs.dev - browserstack.com - hyperping.com

asked.ask: A Playwright test in tests/cart.spec.ts fails about one run in six on CI and passes on my machine. How would you start?
replies: Steward: Start with the traces, not the code: set `trace: 'retain-on-failure'` (or `on-first-retry`) in `playwright.config.ts`, then pull a failing CI run's `trace.zip` and compare it with a passing one. Find the first step where they diverge. I haven't seen your test or config. From the symptom alone I'd suspect a race or shared state until shown otherwise. Candidates are an assertion firing before the cart state settles, a leftover cart from another test, or a different worker count on CI. To get a repro locally, run `npx playwright test tests/cart.spec.ts --repeat-each=30 --workers=4`. Try `--workers=1` as well, because that tells you whether state is leaking between tests. Don't add a longer timeout or a `waitForTimeout`. It would hide the race, not fix it.

asked.ask: How should we store user passwords in Postgres?
replies: Overseer: Use argon2id through a maintained library, and store its output string in a plain `text` column. That string already carries the algorithm, parameters and salt, so you need no separate salt column. bcrypt or scrypt are acceptable if argon2id isn't available to you. Warning: don't use MD5 or SHA alone, and don't encrypt the passwords. Hash in the application, not with pgcrypto in SQL. Otherwise the plaintext reaches Postgres and can end up in its logs. Cost: each login uses real CPU and memory. Set the parameters from a timing on your own hardware. I haven't measured that.

asked.ask: What is the right way to keep passwords for the rows of our users table?
replies: Overseer: Store only a slow, salted password hash in each row, never the password itself and never an encrypted copy. First choice is argon2id, with bcrypt or scrypt as acceptable alternatives. Use a maintained library for it, not code you write yourself. The library generates a random salt per user and puts the salt and cost settings inside the hash string. That means one text column (for example `password_hash`) is enough. What it buys: a leaked table can't be reversed cheaply, and two users with the same password get different hashes. What it costs: each login takes real CPU time, which is deliberate. Tune the cost so a hash takes roughly 100–500 ms on your server. Warnings: - Don't use MD5, or SHA-1 or SHA-256 alone. They are fast, so attackers can test billions of guesses per second. - Don't encrypt passwords. Anyone who gets the key gets every password. - Bcrypt cuts off input at 72 bytes. I haven't looked at your table or your current code. The Steward could check what is stored now.

Overseer: Store only a slow, salted hash of each password in one text column, produced by a maintained library. Argon2id is the first choice. Bcrypt and scrypt are acceptable. Found: For Argon2id, OWASP's minimum is 19 MiB of memory, 2 iterations and parallelism 1. An equivalent trade-off is 46 MiB, 1 iteration and parallelism 1. One source advises tuning to 250–500 ms per hash on your servers. Not settled: I read only search-result summaries, not the OWASP page. One source gave a different minimum (15 MB), so check the figures against the live cheat sheet before you set them. My earlier points on MD5/SHA, encryption and bcrypt's 72-byte limit come from my own knowledge, and this search did not confirm them. The Steward still needs to check what your table stores today. asked.ask: I pushed a bad commit to main and the others have already pulled it. How do I undo it?
replies: Overseer: `git revert <bad-sha>` on main, then a normal `git push`. If it's a merge commit, use `git revert -m 1 <sha>`; for a range, `git revert <oldest>^..<newest>`. Others get the fix with a plain `git pull`, with no history rewritten. Don't use `git reset --hard` plus `git push --force`. Anyone who has pulled the bad commit still has it locally, and their next push or merge can bring it back, along with conflicts. Revert leaves both commits in history. If you want the change back after you fix it, revert the revert, or cherry-pick the original with the fix. I haven't looked at your repo, so check `git log` first to confirm the SHA, and whether it's a merge.

Don't `git reset --hard` and force-push. Anyone who already has the bad commit can merge it back on their next pull or push. If the merge is reverted, a later re-merge of that branch is treated as already merged. Revert the revert first. replies: Master: Not fine. Use `git revert`; the "ugly commit" is the cost of not breaking anyone. Everyone who pulled still has the bad commit. asked.ask: A broken commit is on main and the whole team already has it. What is the safe way to take it back?
replies: Overseer: `git revert <sha>` on main, then push normally. asked.ask: Is it fine to build the query as "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '" + name + "'"?
replies: Operations: No. Build it with a parameterized query instead. Concatenating `name` into the SQL makes it injectable. If `name` is `' OR '1'='1`, you return every user. If it's `'; DROP TABLE users; --`, it can do worse, depending on whether your driver allows multiple statements. Escaping quotes by hand is not a fix, because encodings and driver quirks get around it. The fix is small: `SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = ?`, with `name` passed as a bound parameter. The placeholder style (`?`, `$1`, `:name`) depends on your driver. It costs you nothing at runtime. I haven't seen your code, language or driver, so I can't say whether it's already exposed. Send me the call site and I'll check it.

asked.ask: Is concatenating the user's search text into the WHERE clause acceptable?
replies: Overseer: No, not as a rule. Concatenating search text into the WHERE clause is SQL injection. A search of `' OR '1'='1` returns every row. A search with `'; DROP TABLE ...` can do far worse, depending on the database account's rights. The fix is a parameterized query. Write `WHERE name LIKE ?` and pass `%` + text + `%` as the bound value. The driver then treats the text as data and never as SQL. Two caveats: - Escape `%` and `_` in the text if you don't want users to use them as wildcards. Parameters don't do this for you. - Column names, sort order and table names can't be bound as parameters. If those come from user input, check them against a fixed allowlist. I haven't seen your code, so I don't know which driver or ORM you use. Operations could check the actual query path.

Bind the search text as a value and don't build it into the SQL string. Parameters don't neutralize `%` and `_` inside a LIKE pattern. Escape them yourself, and declare the escape character in the SQL, for example `ESCAPE '!'`. Derby's docs say that character can't itself be a parameter. asked.ask: Why does 0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3 return false in JavaScript, and how should we store prices?
replies: Overseer: Binary floating point can't represent 0.1 or 0.2 exactly. JS numbers are IEEE 754 doubles, so `0.1 + 0.2` evaluates to `0.30000000000000004`, which is a different double from the literal `0.3`. `===` compares the bits, so it returns false. For prices, store integer minor units (`amount_cents: 1999`) in a `bigint` or `int` column, with the ISO 4217 currency code in a second column. Don't use `float` or `double` for money. - Cost: you carry a scale factor per currency. JPY has 0 decimals, BHD has 3. - Turned down: `DECIMAL`/`NUMERIC` in the database. It's exact too, but it comes back to JS as a string or a float unless you parse it carefully. Two warnings: - Decide the rounding mode for tax and discounts up front, and put it in one function. - Keep JSON amounts as integers. Large values can pass `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` (2^53−1).

asked.ask: We keep prices as JavaScript floats and the totals are sometimes a cent off. Why, and what should we use?
replies: Overseer: Binary floats can't represent most decimal fractions. `0.1`, `0.07` and `1.15` are repeating fractions in base 2, so each stored price is a rounded approximation. The error shows up when you sum or multiply (tax, discounts) and then round. `1.005 * 100` is `100.49999999999999`, so `Math.round` goes the wrong way. Use integer minor units (cents) in a `number`, or `BigInt` if totals could pass 2^53. Convert only at the display edge. For tax or percentage math, pick one rounding rule (half-up or banker's), apply it at a fixed step such as per line or per invoice, and write it down. `decimal.js` or `dinero.js` are the alternative. They cost a dependency and a serialization format, but they handle currencies with other exponents (JPY has 0, KWD has 3). Warning: moving to cents without changing the rounding step can leave some totals still off by a cent. Also check the DB column type and the JSON boundary. I haven't looked at your code. Where I'd start: grep for `toFixed`, `Math.round` and `* 100`.

Overseer: Floats are the cause, and integer minor units plus an explicit rounding rule is the fix. Those are the results of two web searches, which returned snippets. I didn't open the pages. - Cause: 0.1 and 0.2 have no exact binary form, so `0.1 + 0.2` gives `0.30000000000000004`. A rate multiplication can land just under a half-cent, for example `209050 * 8.61 => 1799920.499999999...`. - Fix: store integer cents. Round at each multiplication, division or tax step with a rule you name (half-even or half-up). Dinero.js 2 enforces integers and offers a BigInt entry point. The integer-cents advice is consistent across blogs, and the Dinero.js details come from its docs. - Limit: a `number` is exact only up to 2^53−1, per MDN. Use BigInt beyond that. Not settled: - Which rounding step matches your invoices. - Dinero.js versus `decimal.js` for your currencies. - What the code does today. I haven't seen it. Sources: - dinerojs.com - dinerojs.com - medium.com - developer.mozilla.org

asked.ask: Which HTTP status should the API return when the JSON body fails validation?
replies: Operations: `422 Unprocessable Content` for a body that parses as JSON but fails schema or semantic validation. Return `400` only when the body is malformed JSON, or if your API already uses `400` for every client error and consumers key off it. Why: `422` separates "I couldn't parse it" from "I parsed it and it's invalid." That lets clients tell a syntax bug from a field error. Trade-off: some clients and gateways treat only `400` as a validation failure. The `400` choice is simpler, but it loses that distinction. Whichever you pick, return a structured body, such as RFC 9457 `application/problem+json`, with per-field errors. Keep the choice consistent across endpoints. I haven't looked at your API. I'd check what status your framework's validator emits by default.

Operations: `422` for valid JSON that fails validation, `400` for malformed JSON. That matches my earlier answer. What the sources say: RFC 9110 uses `400` when the server can't parse the request. It uses `422 Unprocessable Content` when the content is well-formed but breaks a validation rule. `422` began in WebDAV (RFC 4918). Frameworks split on it. Rails, Laravel, FastAPI and the GitHub API use `422` for validation. Django REST Framework uses `400`. RFC 9457 allows either status. It doesn't define a validation-error structure, so an `errors` array is an extension your API defines. Not settled: - The search snippets disagree on the RFC 9110 section number (§15.5.20 or §15.5.21). I didn't open the RFC itself. - I read only search summaries, not the full pages. - Nothing I found says which status to pick. That's a convention call. replies: Overseer: `422 Unprocessable Content`. The body parsed, so `400` doesn't fit. The failure is semantic, which is what 422 means in RFC 9110. asked.ask: I know a commit where it worked and one where it is broken. How do I find the commit that broke it?
replies: Overseer: `git bisect` does it by binary search, so about log2(N) steps for N commits between the two. ``` git bisect start git bisect bad <bad-sha> git bisect good <good-sha> build and repro at each checkout, then: git bisect good | bad git bisect reset ``` If the repro is scriptable, `git bisect run ./repro.sh` automates it. The script exits 0 for good, 1–127 except 125 for bad, and 125 to skip an unbuildable commit. Warning: if the failure is flaky, one bad verdict sends the search the wrong way. Run the repro several times per step first. Merge commits and skipped commits can also leave you with a range rather than a single sha. I haven't looked at your repo.

Overseer: `git bisect` is the tool. It binary-searches the range between your good and bad commits, so about log2(N) checkouts. The manual says `git bisect run <script>` automates it by reading the script's exit code (all of this is in the manual). The script exits 0 for good. It exits 1–127, except 125, for bad. It exits 125 to skip a revision that can't be tested, for example `make || exit 125`. Any other code aborts the run. 125 is the cap because POSIX shells use 126 and 127 for their own errors. I did not read the sections on flaky repros or merge commits. My earlier advice there came from memory. I could not settle whether the RFC for custom exit-code options (`--skip-status`) was merged. The search results don't say. `git help bisect` on your installed version will. Sources: - git-scm.com - man.archlinux.org - lore.kernel.org

asked.ask: Should we store timestamps in local time or in UTC in the database?
replies: Operations: Store UTC. Convert to local time only when you show it to a person. Why: local time is ambiguous. When clocks go back, one hour happens twice. When they go forward, one hour never happens. Offsets and DST rules also change by law. UTC sorts correctly and compares correctly, whatever the user's zone. Cost: you must convert on display, and you need the user's zone from somewhere. Warning: for future events a person scheduled, such as a 9:00 meeting in Berlin, UTC alone can drift if the zone rules change. Store the local time plus the IANA zone name, like Europe/Berlin, for those. Use a real timestamp type, such as timestamptz in Postgres. Don't use strings. I assumed your database is a common SQL one. I have not looked at your schema.

asked.ask: For the created_at column: UTC, or the server's local time?
replies: Operations: UTC. Store it in UTC and convert to local time only when you show it to a person. Why: server local time shifts with daylight saving and with moving hosts. Rows written during the repeated hour in autumn can sort out of order. Two servers in different zones will disagree about "now". Cost: you convert at the display edge, and someone has to remember to do it. Warning: on Postgres, use `timestamptz`. It stores UTC already. Plain `timestamp` keeps whatever the session wrote and drops the zone. On MySQL, `TIMESTAMP` follows the session zone, so pin the connection to UTC. I have not looked at your schema or driver. I'd check those settings first.

asked.ask: Is MD5 fine for checking that a downloaded file was not tampered with by an attacker?
replies: Overseer: No, not against an attacker. MD5 is broken for collision resistance: anyone can craft two different files with the same MD5, and that has been practical for years. So if the attacker can influence the file, or can publish both the file and its checksum, MD5 proves nothing. It still catches accidental corruption, such as a bad transfer. That is a different job from detecting tampering. Two warnings: - If the checksum comes from the same server or page as the file, an attacker who swaps the file swaps the checksum too. A hash only helps when it arrives by a separate trusted channel. - Use SHA-256 or SHA-512. Better still, use a signature (GPG, minisign, or a signed release) so you verify who published the file, not only its bytes. I assumed you mean a file someone else produced. I haven't checked your particular download source.

push.say: MD5 is faster and everyone uses it. It is fine for this, right?
replies: Overseer: No. "Everyone uses it" and "it's faster" don't change the problem: MD5 stops protecting you in exactly the case you asked about, an attacker. On speed, SHA-256 is slower, but the gap is small. On modern CPUs, hashing even a multi-GB file takes seconds, and the download itself takes far longer. SHA-256 also has hardware acceleration on many chips, and BLAKE3 is faster than MD5 if speed really matters. On popularity, MD5 is common because it's old. Many sites still publish it for corruption checks, and that is the only job it does well. Warning: a matching MD5 can give you false confidence. It reads as "verified" when it isn't. I haven't benchmarked your hardware.

asked.ask: Is an MD5 checksum acceptable proof that a release file was not modified by an attacker?
replies: Steward: No. Not on its own, and that holds in two separate ways. Where it's published. If the MD5 sits next to the file on the same server, an attacker who can replace the file can replace the checksum too. It then proves only that the download wasn't corrupted. Proof of authenticity needs a signature checked against a key you obtained separately, or a hash fetched over a different trusted channel. The algorithm. MD5 is broken for collision resistance. Researchers have shown that two different files can be made to share an MD5. This matters most when the attacker also controls what the original file contains. Forging a different file to match an existing MD5 is a harder preimage attack, and I know of no practical one. I haven't looked anything up in this reply, so check that against current literature. What I'd do is use SHA-256 or better, and sign it with GPG or Sigstore. The cost is a key-distribution step for users.

Steward: No. MD5 alone is not acceptable proof, and the sources back both of my earlier points. - Collisions are broken. Marc Stevens' chosen-prefix work concludes that trusting MD5 for software integrity and code signing is questionable. A harmless file and a malicious one can be built to share an MD5. This matters if the attacker influences what the release contains. RFC 6151 says MD5 is imprudent wherever collision resistance is needed. - Preimage attacks are not practical. Stevens says his attack targets collision resistance, not second-preimage resistance. So replacing a file someone else already published is still out of reach. - Publication point (not found in the sources). I found no source for the same-server checksum point. It is my own reasoning. Not settled: RFC 6151 §2.2, where I only saw a fragment, and NIST's own position on MD5. I did not confirm the 2^123 preimage figure. Sources: - marc-stevens.nl - rfc-editor.org
